planting.note: Plant rooted suckers or container stock in spring into average to dry, well-drained soil in full to partial sun; this tough plains shrub tolerates heavy clay, drought, and cold with ease.

directions: Plant rooted suckers or nursery stock in spring in average to dry soil and full to partial sun, spacing plants to allow the colony to spread naturally by underground rhizomes into a dense thicket. Western snowberry needs little care once established and tolerates heavy clay, drought, and harsh prairie winters better than most ornamental shrubs. Small pink-tinged bell flowers in early summer draw bumblebees and other native pollinators, and the waxy white berries that follow persist into winter, feeding sharp-tailed grouse, pheasants, and small mammals when other food is scarce. The dense, thicket-forming habit also provides valuable nesting and escape cover for grassland songbirds.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Plant rooted layers or container stock in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this low, sprawling shrub of Pacific Coast forests roots readily where trailing stems touch soil.

directions: Plant rooted stem sections or nursery starts in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, letting the trailing stems spread and root along the ground to knit together a low, informal groundcover under trees. Trailing snowberry is native to open woods and coastal bluffs of the Pacific Northwest and California, where its sprawling form stabilizes soil on slopes and forest edges. Small pinkish flowers in early summer attract native bees, and the round white berries that follow are eaten by grouse, quail, and small mammals through the colder months. Its dense low cover also shelters ground-feeding birds and provides forage for browsing deer.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; sweet crabapple prefers open sites at woodland edges and old fields.

directions: Plant young trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil and full sun to light shade, choosing an open site at a field or woodland edge where the rounded crown has room to spread. Sweet crabapple, native to the eastern and midwestern United States, produces intensely fragrant pale pink blossoms in mid-spring that draw large numbers of native bees and other pollinators before most other trees have leafed out. The small, hard, greenish-yellow fruit ripens in fall and often clings into winter, becoming an important food source for foxes, deer, and overwintering birds such as robins and cedar waxwings once it softens after frost. Its dense branching also offers good nesting cover for songbirds.

planting.note: Plant young trees in spring into well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun; prairie crabapple is adapted to the fencerows, savannas, and old fields of the tallgrass prairie region and tolerates drought once rooted.

directions: Plant young trees in spring in well-drained, average to dry soil and full sun, giving the thorny, wide-spreading crown room in an open fencerow, savanna, or pasture edge planting. Prairie crabapple is more drought tolerant than many crabapples once established, reflecting its origin on the tallgrass prairie and midwestern plains. Its very fragrant, rose-pink blossoms open in late spring and are heavily worked by native bees, while the small, waxy, greenish-yellow fruit persists into winter and is eaten by foxes, raccoons, deer, and fruit-eating birds after repeated freezing and thawing softens it. Dense, thorny branching also offers secure nesting sites for grassland and edge-dwelling birds.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in spring into cool, moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this boreal native prefers cooler climates and struggles in hot, humid summers.

directions: Plant young trees in spring in cool, moist, well-drained, acidic soil and full sun to light shade, sited where summers stay relatively cool since this northern species declines in hot, humid regions. Showy mountain ash is native to boreal forests, rocky shorelines, and cold uplands across the northern United States and Canada, forming a small, rounded tree with flat clusters of white spring flowers that attract bees and other pollinators. The large, bright orange-red berry clusters ripen in early fall and persist into winter, becoming a magnet for migrating and overwintering cedar waxwings, pine grosbeaks, and other winter finches once softened by frost. Its open branching structure also provides good perching and nesting sites for songbirds.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall into lean, fast-draining, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; snowbrush ceanothus is a fire-adapted native of dry western forests and resents rich, wet, or heavily amended soil.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall into lean, fast-draining, rocky soil in full sun, choosing a dry slope or open site similar to the burned or disturbed forest ground this species naturally colonizes across the mountain West. Snowbrush ceanothus fixes atmospheric nitrogen at its roots, allowing it to thrive in poor soils where it also improves fertility for neighboring plants. Its dense, fragrant clusters of small white flowers in early summer are among the most heavily visited native shrub blooms for bees, butterflies, and other pollinators, while deer and elk browse the evergreen foliage and small mammals and birds eat the seed. The thick, glossy leaves and low, spreading form also provide valuable cover for ground-nesting birds.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall into well-drained, gravelly to loamy soil in full sun to light shade; this Pacific Northwest native colonizes open woods, streambanks, and recently disturbed or burned forest ground.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall into well-drained, gravelly to loamy soil in full sun to light shade, giving the upright, reddish-stemmed canes room along a streambank, open woodland edge, or recently cleared site. Redstem ceanothus is named for its distinctive maroon-red young bark, which stands out clearly against the surrounding forest even in winter. Dense conical clusters of fragrant white flowers open in late spring and are worked heavily by native bees, butterflies, and other pollinating insects, while deer and elk browse the twigs and foliage and grouse and small mammals eat the seed. It readily resprouts after fire or cutting, making it valuable early cover and forage in recovering forest habitat.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Plant rooted suckers, cuttings, or container stock in spring into average, well-drained soil in full to partial sun; Wood's rose is widespread across western and central North America and tolerates cold, drought, and poor soil.

directions: Plant rooted suckers or nursery stock in spring in average, well-drained soil and full to partial sun, allowing room for the thicket-forming shrub to spread by underground rhizomes into a dense, thorny colony. Wood's rose ranges from the Great Plains to the Pacific Coast and from Canada into Mexico, tolerating cold winters, drought, and poor soils better than most cultivated roses. Its fragrant pink single flowers in early summer feed native bees, and the bright red hips that follow persist through winter, providing critical food for grouse, pheasants, and songbirds along with browse for deer. The dense, prickly thickets also create some of the safest nesting cover available to grassland and shrubland birds.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings, suckers, or container stock in spring into moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Nootka rose is native to the Pacific coast and understory margins from California to Alaska.

directions: Plant rooted suckers or nursery stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil and full sun to light shade, spacing plants to allow the arching canes to form an informal thicket along a woodland edge, hedgerow, or streambank. Nootka rose is native to the Pacific Coast from northern California to Alaska, where it grows in open forest, coastal bluffs, and moist thickets. Its large, fragrant pink flowers, among the showiest of the wild roses, open in early summer and attract native bees, and the unusually large red hips that follow are an important winter food for grouse, thrushes, and small mammals as well as browse for deer. Dense, thorny growth also provides secure nesting habitat for shrub-nesting songbirds.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in fall into well-drained, rocky to loamy soil in partial sun; mallow ninebark is native to dry montane forest understories of the Pacific Northwest and Northern Rockies.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in fall into well-drained, rocky to loamy soil in partial sun, matching the dry, open coniferous forest understory this species naturally inhabits across the Northern Rockies and Pacific Northwest. Mallow ninebark forms a dense, rounded mound of maple-like lobed leaves with clusters of small white to pinkish flowers in early summer that draw native bees and other pollinating insects. Its inflated seed capsules are eaten by songbirds through fall, while the foliage and twigs are browsed by deer and elk, making it an important component of wildlife habitat in dry western forests. Peeling, multi-layered bark gives the shrub interest through the winter months and shelter for overwintering insects.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)
